column4: Rain makes valleys flow according to their measure, while the flood carries swelling foam; this directly gathers the section's valley-channel, overflow, measure, and passing-foam image.
The earth is burst into springs in وَفَجَّرْنَا ٱلْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا and the two waters meet upon a decreed affair, directly joining gushing with prior measure.
إِنَّا لَمَّا طَغَا ٱلْمَاءُ uses the section's overflow word literally of floodwater and sets saving carriage within the very water that exceeded its bound.
Stone can gush rivers, split so water emerges, or fall in awe; this is the section's exact reversal of hearts harder than rock and rock opened by water.
Moses strikes the rock, twelve springs burst from it, every people knows its drinking place, and the gift closes with a ban on spreading corruption.
The struck rock bursts into twelve springs and each tribe knows its watering place, tying gushing provision to an apportioned communal measure.
Water descends from heaven بِقَدَرٍ, is lodged in the earth, and can be taken away; the ayah states the section's life-giving water held to measure and divine control.
If provision were expanded without limit people would transgress, so God sends it in the measure He wills; this makes moral overflow and measured rizq one claim.
أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا ٱلْمَاءَ صَبًّا uses the same pouring verb as the punishment in the section, but the object poured from above is merciful water.
The earth is then split open emphatically, reversing the destructive downward pouring into soil opened for growth.
Wind bears heavy cloud, water descends, fruit comes forth, and dead land models the raising of the dead; it states the full rain-life-return sequence developed in the section.
ʿĀd sees a cloud advancing toward its valleys and calls it rain, but it is the hastened wind containing painful punishment: the expected sweet water becomes chastisement.
The flood of the dam replaces Saba's two fruitful gardens with bitter produce, showing water past its bound sweeping away the provision water had sustained.
Corruption appears on land and sea through human deeds, giving the section's imbalance a literal terrestrial and maritime spread.
Thamūd is settled in the land, builds on its plains, carves mountain homes, and is told not to roam as corrupters; this directly reunites rock dwelling and fasād.
Boiling water يُصَبُّ مِن فَوْقِ رُءُوسِهِمْ is poured from above their heads, a precise punitive reversal of rain using the section's pouring verb.
صُبُّوا فَوْقَ رَأْسِهِۦ مِنْ عَذَابِ ٱلْحَمِيمِ explicitly joins pouring from above, punishment, and scalding water in one command.
The demanded sign is a date-and-grape garden with rivers forcefully gushed through it, exactly the human demand for controlled abundance recalled by the section.
God's servants drink from a spring that يُفَجِّرُونَهَا تَفْجِيرًا, transferring the act of making water gush to the people admitted to divine provision.
وَإِذَا ٱلْبِحَارُ فُجِّرَتْ expands the same bursting-open action from a spring or river to the seas at the final unmaking.
The ayah places those who spread corruption on earth against the God-fearing and names the opposite party ٱلْفُجَّارِ, directly meeting both secondary roots developed in the section.
بَلْ يُرِيدُ ٱلْإِنسَانُ لِيَفْجُرَ أَمَامَهُ pictures the human wanting to break forward into sin, closely matching the source dictionary sense of opening and launching into disobedience.
أَلَّا تَطْغَوْا فِى ٱلْمِيزَانِ forbids overflowing the balance itself, turning the section's water beyond measure into an exact moral rule.
وَفِى ٱلسَّمَاءِ رِزْقُكُمْ locates provision in the sky, supporting the source dictionary claim that rain can be called rizq.
The oath by وَٱلسَّمَاءِ ذَاتِ ٱلرَّجْعِ supplies the source section's secondary sense of rajʿ as repeatedly returning rain beside the soul's commanded return.
Water is sent from heaven بِقَدَرٍ, dead land is revived, and human emergence is compared to it; measure, life, and return are explicit together.
Every thing has divine treasuries and descends only بِقَدَرٍ مَّعْلُومٍ, giving the governing rule behind measured rain and restricted provision.
Fertilizing winds precede water sent from the sky for drink, while humans are not its storekeepers; provision descends and remains outside their control.
Unexpected provision, trust in God's sufficiency, and قَدْ جَعَلَ ٱللَّهُ لِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ قَدْرًا join rizq with a divinely set measure for everything.
God expands and restricts provision, while people rejoice in the nearer life that is only slight beside the Hereafter; this directly corrects the human reading in 89:16.
The well-provided spends from abundance and the one whose provision is restricted spends from what God gave; restriction is followed by promised ease, not humiliation.
Rain is sent after people despair and divine mercy is spread, correcting the judgment that delayed or narrowed provision means rejection.
Steadfastness on the path would bring abundant water, making water itself the concrete form of expanded provision.
The abundant water of the preceding ayah is explicitly a test, matching the section's insistence that provision is trial rather than proof of honor.
Saba has two gardens, is told to eat its Lord's provision, and is given a good land and forgiving Lord; garden growth and rizq are joined before the flood.
The spoiled gardens are requital for ingratitude, locating the loss of watery abundance in response rather than in an automatic verdict of humiliation.
Former generations received abundant rain and rivers, yet were destroyed for their sins; the same water-given power and later ruin form the section's historical current.
Hūd promises his people abundant rain and added strength if they seek forgiveness, so the people who mistook punishment for rain are also offered rain as mercy.
Blessed water descends from the sky and grows gardens and harvested grain, directly realizing water poured down as provision.
Tall date palms with layered clusters specify the garden growth produced by the blessed water in 50:9.
The crop is provision for servants, dead land is revived with water, and خروج is the likeness for resurrection; growth, rizq, life, and emergence meet explicitly.
God sends water down, channels it as springs in the earth, brings varied crops, then they yellow and become debris; the full course shows what flows, flourishes, and passes.
Worldly life is water from heaven mingling with earth's growth until people think they command it, when a divine command leaves it mown; abundance never proves ownership.
Worldly life is likened to rain-grown vegetation that becomes wind-scattered dry matter, setting passing growth against the One who retains power.
Worldly rivalry in increase is paired with rain whose growth delights, then withers and becomes debris; numerical swelling and water-fed transience share one image.
وَأَنزَلْنَا مِنَ ٱلْمُعْصِرَاتِ مَاءً ثَجَّاجًا gives the image of water pouring profusely from rainclouds.
The purpose of that poured water is to bring forth grain and vegetation, identifying abundance as provided food.
Dense gardens are the final product of the descending water, matching the section's movement from rain to flourishing janna.
The command فَلْيَنظُرِ ٱلْإِنسَانُ إِلَىٰ طَعَامِهِ frames the pouring and splitting in 80:25-26 as a lesson about the food a human calls provision.
Grain is the first named growth brought out after water is poured and earth is split.
Grapes and fresh herbage extend the concrete produce of the opened, watered ground.
Olive and date palm show the continuing conversion of poured water into lasting food-bearing plants.
وَحَدَائِقَ غُلْبًا names luxuriant gardens as the flourishing outcome toward which the section's final janna image moves.
Fruit and pasture complete the range of products brought from the watered earth.
مَتَاعًا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ states that the whole rain-growth sequence is provision for humans and their livestock.
Water descends from the sky and brings fruits as provision, a direct Qur'anic realization of rain being called rizq.
God sends water from heaven, brings fruits as provision, and subjects rivers, linking descending water, food, and flowing channels.
Water from heaven supplies drink and the vegetation in which livestock pasture, presenting the two recipients of measured rain.
The same water grows crops, olives, dates, grapes, and every fruit, filling out the section's garden-from-rain image.
Winds herald mercy and pure water is sent from the sky, the beneficent cloud-scene opposite ʿĀd's fatal expectation.
The pure water revives a dead land and gives drink to animals and many people, joining life and apportioned sustenance.
What God sends from heaven is explicitly called رِزْقٍ and revives earth after death, uniting the source's rain-rizq and rain-life dictionary senses.
God shows signs and sends provision from the sky; the wording directly supports the section's reading of descending rain as rizq.
Water from heaven revives earth after death, while winds and clouds are directed between heaven and earth; it sets the complete ordered water system as a sign.
Water sent from heaven gives life to earth after its death, stating the source dictionary explanation of rain as ḥayā.
Asked who sends water and thereby revives dead earth, the addressees must answer God; control of life-giving rain cannot be inferred from human status.
Lightning brings fear and hope, water descends from heaven, and dead earth lives; expected rain is held between promise and danger.
Winds raise cloud, cloud is driven to dead land, and earth revives; the ayah then identifies this as the resurrection.
The humbled earth stirs and swells when water descends, and its reviver is declared able to revive the dead.
Rain makes lifeless earth stir, swell, and grow every lovely pair, giving a bodily scene for resurrection through water.
Dead earth is revived and yields grain people eat, making life and food the paired effects of water's hidden work.
Gardens of dates and grapes are made and springs are burst within them, explicitly linking janna and tafjīr.
People eat the garden's fruit although their hands did not make it, challenging possession-based readings of provision.
Water from heaven brings every vegetation, grain, dates, grapes, olives, and pomegranates; looking at fruit and ripening makes provision's growth the sign.
Neighboring plots, vineyards, crops, and palms are watered with one water yet differ in produce, showing that measured difference is divine ordering rather than disgrace.
Earth is made a bed with paths, water descends, and diverse plants are brought out, joining habitable ground, channels, and provision.
Humans eat and pasture livestock from that growth, identifying the rain scene's practical provision.
With measured water God produces date-and-grape gardens containing abundant fruits, so measure culminates in janna and food.
Water is driven to barren land and crops emerge for livestock and people to eat, a direct scene of hidden provision becoming visible.
Winds raise and spread clouds, rain comes through them, and people rejoice when it reaches whom God wills; the ayah stages the cloud's true merciful face.
The hearer is commanded to look at the effects of mercy in earth's revival, which is then made evidence for reviving the dead.
Clouds are driven, joined, and heaped before rain emerges, while hail may strike or be turned away; the same sky-bearing form holds measured benefit and harm.
The river is made an explicit test and drinking from it is limited to a small allowance, joining water, measure, and trial in one scene.
Thamūd is told that water is apportioned between them and the she-camel, with each drinking turn attended; measured water becomes the covenant they cross.
The she-camel has one drinking share and the people another on a known day, placing Thamūd's conduct under a precise water measure.
God's messenger names the she-camel and her drink as the boundary Thamūd must honor.
They deny, hamstring the camel, and are crushed for their sin, showing destruction after violating the measured water arrangement.
Nine men in the city spread corruption rather than set things right, supplying the organized fasād of Thamūd behind the rock-city's end.
Their houses lie empty because of wrongdoing, making the carved dwelling itself the remnant of a community that exceeded its bounds.
Thamūd carves houses from mountains with confident skill, the closest parallel to cutting rock in the valley.
They carve mountain houses feeling secure, sharpening the section's contrast between engineered rock shelter and an unmastered divine judgment.
Pharaoh's people are seized with years of drought and diminished fruits so they might remember, making restricted provision a sign rather than humiliation.
They claim good provision as their due and treat hardship as an omen from Moses, closely matching the human error of reading provision as a status verdict.
The flood is among the detailed signs sent against Pharaoh's arrogant criminal people, joining tyranny with literal overwhelming water.
The sea is parted to save Israel and drown Pharaoh's people before their eyes; one body of water is measured mercy and sweeping judgment.
Moses is commanded to strike a dry path through the sea without fearing pursuit or drowning, showing water held back for rescue.
Pharaoh follows and the sea covers his force, so the restrained water returns as judgment upon the transgressor.
The sea splits after Moses strikes it and each part stands like a huge mountain, an immense counterpart to rock splitting for springs.
Moses and his companions are saved, then the others are drowned; the same divided water distinguishes mercy from punishment.
When Pharaoh's people provoke divine anger, all are drowned, turning imperial overflow into engulfment by water.
Pharaoh and his hosts are seized and flung into the sea, a concrete water-ending for the ruler listed among the section's overflowers.
Pharaoh tries to drive the people from the land, so he and those with him are drowned, joining aggression in the land with water judgment.
After denying the signs, Pharaoh's people are drowned in the sea; the destructive water is expressly tied to their heedlessness.
The affluent boast that greater wealth and children exempt them from punishment, stating the false status inference implicit in “my Lord honored me.”
The answer is that God expands and restricts provision, but most people do not know; abundance therefore cannot certify favor.
The question asks whether wealth and children are being hurried to people as good, exposing the same misreading of expanded provision.
بَل لَّا يَشْعُرُونَ denies their perception, confirming that material increase is not a transparent divine verdict.
The garden owners are explicitly tested as they resolve to harvest, making a fruitful garden itself the form of trial.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep, showing provision withdrawn outside their control.
By morning the garden is like a field already reaped, the sudden loss reversing its expected fruitfulness.
The owners finally say they have been deprived, voicing the human perception of narrowed provision after the garden vanishes.
They confess إِنَّا كُنَّا طَاغِينَ, naming their own moral overflow within the garden-and-provision test.
One sea is عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ, sweet and pleasant, and the other salty and bitter, with a barrier between; it gives the exact sweet-water sense placed beside ʿadhāb in the source.
The two seas are explicitly unequal: one is عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ and easy to drink, the other salty and bitter, making sweetness a bounded water quality.
The promised garden has rivers of unspoiled water and other drinks, while the opposing people drink boiling water that cuts their bowels; provision and punishment share a liquid form.
The hearer is asked to consider the water being drunk, opening a direct challenge to claims of possession over provision.
The next question asks whether humans sent it from the raincloud or God did, assigning the downward gift to its true giver.
God could make the water bitter, so drinkable sweetness is a contingent mercy rather than an entitlement.
If water sinks away, no one besides God can bring flowing water; the hidden-source scene reverses confident possession of provision.
A garden's water may sink so deeply that its owner cannot seek it, exposing the fragility of apparent abundance.
A downpour strips the thin soil from a hard rock and leaves it bare, reversing the section's rock that opens to release water and making rain disclose empty action.
The rejecters ask for stones to be rained from heaven or painful punishment if the message is true, perversely requesting punishment in rain's place.
A punitive rain falls on Lot's people, making rain itself the vehicle of the criminals' end rather than of life.
The overturned towns receive a rain of layered baked stones, a descending judgment opposed to the water that opens earth for crops.
After the town is overturned, baked stones rain upon it; the downward shower realizes punishment rather than provision.
The rain upon the warned people is called an evil rain, explicitly marking the reversal of the cloud's expected gift.
An evil rain falls on those who were warned, again placing chastisement in the form normally awaited as mercy.
The wind destroys everything by its Lord's command until only dwellings remain, completing 46:24's reversal from expected raincloud to erasing judgment.
A furious wind gives ʿĀd a humiliating punishment in worldly life, distinguishing actual humiliation from the imagined humiliation of restricted provision.
ʿĀd is destroyed by a clamorous, furious wind, identifying the force hidden inside the cloud they called rain.
The wind is imposed for seven nights and eight days and leaves people like hollow palm trunks, extending the destructive aftermath of the false rain expectation.
A screaming wind is sent on a day of continuous ill fortune, the punishing answer to ʿĀd's cloud reading.
The wind uproots people like torn palm trunks, replacing the growth expected from rain with uprooting.
The wind sent against ʿĀd is explicitly barren, a precise opposite to the fertilizing rain-bearing wind.
That wind leaves whatever it touches like decayed matter, completing the reversal from water-fed flourishing to desiccation.
Hell gives the obstinate tyrant foul water to drink, turning water from sustaining gift into punishment.
He tries to swallow it as death comes from every side without ending him, intensifying the boundary between life-giving drink and punitive liquid.
The transgressors taste neither coolness nor drink in hell, a deprivation of the two mercies associated with water.
Only boiling fluid and foul discharge answer that deprivation, making liquid itself a fitting punitive counterpart.
The unbelievers demand that a spring be made to gush from the earth; it is a direct tafjīr scene, though framed as a coercive demand for a sign.
The soul is inspired with its fujūr and its taqwā, placing the source dictionary's “opening into sin” against an inward moral boundary.
The wicked are named ٱلْفُجَّارِ in the same surah whose seas are burst open at 82:3, letting the two Qur'anic branches of the root sound within one judgment scene.
Noah's people are drowned because of their sins and then admitted to fire, concretely joining moral transgression to overwhelming water.
Within the Noah setting, the feared offspring is described as فَاجِرًا كَفَّارًا, supplying the sin branch of the same root beside the flood narrative.
The record of the fujjār is placed in Sijjīn; this carries the developed sin sense of the root into a reckoning context parallel to surah 89.
At judgment the faces are those of ٱلْكَفَرَةُ ٱلْفَجَرَةُ, carrying the root's moral branch into the same surah that earlier pours water and grows food.
God raises the sky and sets the balance, supplying the ordered frame for the following prohibition against overflowing the measure.
The command to establish weight with justice and not diminish the balance gives the positive form of remaining within measure.
Everything is created بِقَدَرٍ, generalizing the section's measured water and measured provision into a rule of creation.
God creates everything and determines it with exact determination, supporting the section's claim that water's effects are governed rather than accidental.
After describing increase and decrease in the womb, the ayah says everything with God is by measure; the connection is the same governing qadar, not a water scene.
Earth's sustenance is apportioned in four days for those who ask, extending measured provision from rain to the created world's food supply.
The Lord expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it, directly repeating the correction to 89:16's interpretation.
After Qarun's collapse, observers recognize that God expands and restricts provision; their revised judgment supplies the correction the section demands.
God expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it, another direct formulation of provision's variable measure.
The addressees are asked whether they see God expanding and restricting provision, treating those changes as signs rather than ranks of honor.
The Lord expands and restricts provision, and whatever is spent is replaced; measured rizq is paired with trust in its giver.
The question asks whether people know God expands and restricts provision; the changes are signs for believers.
The One owning heaven's and earth's keys expands and restricts provision, locating its measure in divine dominion.
God contracts and expands and to Him people return, a compact pairing of changing measure with the return that closes the section.
Seven years of diligent cultivation and stored grain show abundant produce being measured against a coming shortage.
Seven severe years consume what was stored, making restriction part of an ordered cycle rather than a verdict of humiliation.
A later year brings relief by rain and renewed pressing of produce, completing the return from scarcity to provision.
The life-giving water is distributed among people so they may remember, but most respond with ingratitude; distribution and moral response are both measured.
The ban on corrupting earth after it has been set right stands immediately before the rain, fruit, and resurrection scene of 7:57.
Good land brings vegetation by its Lord's leave while bad land yields scantily, showing differing produce under the same divine signs.
Full measure and weight are commanded together with a ban on spreading corruption in the land, joining balance and fasād explicitly.
The command to give full measure begins a passage that opposes quantitative injustice to corruption.
Weighing with an even balance supplies the equilibrium whose loss the section hears in fasād.
Diminishing people's goods and roaming earth as corrupters makes violated measure a form of fasād.
The corruptor destroys crops and offspring, so fasād is shown undoing the living produce that water and earth bring forth.
Pharaoh exalts himself in the land, divides its people, and is called one of the corrupters, specifying the political overflow behind his place in surah 89.
Qarun is told to seek the Hereafter with what God gave, keep a worldly share, and not seek corruption on earth; provision is bounded by moral use.
The final home is for those who seek neither elevation nor corruption on earth, opposing both vertical pride and imbalance.
Every soul returns after being tested with bad and good as trial, supporting the section's correction that either form of provision is an examination.
The people are tested with good things and bad things so they may return, another explicit denial that ease or restriction alone fixes divine status.
Wealth and children are a trial, directly classifying material increase as testing rather than proof of honor.
Solomon calls an extraordinary gift his Lord's favor testing whether he will be grateful, providing the right reading of bestowed abundance.
The parable begins with two grape gardens surrounded by palms and crops, establishing provision in a cultivated enclosure.
Both gardens yield fully and a river is made to gush between them, giving the abundance its watercourse.
The owner has fruit and boasts of greater wealth and followers, turning water-fed produce into a status claim.
He enters his garden wronging himself and claims it will never perish, showing possession mistaken for permanence.
He is told to answer the garden with “What God willed; no power except through God,” the grateful stance missing from status-based readings of provision.
A reckoning from heaven may leave the garden barren and slippery, reversing the assumed security of its abundance.
The fruit is encompassed and its owner wrings his hands over what he spent, completing the collapse of provision treated as permanent rank.
The garden owners finally glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing, showing the moral recognition produced by deprivation.
Hūd warns ʿĀd among the dunes before the cloud appears; it locates 46:24's water expectation in the landscape of the people named by surah 89.
Several peoples are seized by different consequences of sin, including storm, earth-collapse, and drowning; the catalog marks judgment as fitted rather than uncontrolled nature.
Firm mountains and fresh water are placed together as earth's provision, echoing rock, stored water, and drinkable sweetness without using the source's exact root.
The two promised gardens contain two flowing springs, making moving water internal to janna.
Two other gardens contain two gushing springs, a direct non-fajara wording for the section's springing-water scene.
A flowing spring lies within the high garden, joining the section's water motion to its final destination.
Patient servants are rewarded with a garden before the later drink and spring details, setting the home of 76:6's gushing water.
Paradise vessels are measured with exact measure, placing qadar even within the scene of freely given drink.
A spring named Salsabīl supplies the later paradise-drink scene, extending the flowing source introduced at 76:6.
The companions of the right receive poured-out water, a paradise counterpart to water poured as earthly mercy and punishment.
